newsitem.title: JAPAN: Bonus season's non-yen bond issues may aid dollar.
newsitem.headline: Bonus season's non-yen bond issues may aid dollar.

text.p: A flood of non-yen foreign bond issues targeting individual Japanese investors, whose pockets will soon be bulging with summer bonus payments, is likely to buoy the dollar against the yen, market sources say.
"The bonus season is the time when individual investors' assets flow into the financial markets," said a manager in Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd's market planning department.
Most Japanese employees receive bonus payments twice a year, during the summer and at the end of the year.
Yamaichi aims to expand its range of foreign bond offerings, including dual-currency samurai bonds, to attract individual investors flush with cash during the bonus season.
A dual-currency samurai bond allows the holder to earn interest in yen on bonds redeemable in a foreign currency, such as the dollar or the pound.

In April, 250 billion yen ($2.00 billion) worth of dual-currency samurai bonds were issued, up from 115 billion yen ($920 million) in January, underwriting sources said. The issue of dollar- and sterling-based bonds, including bonds with options, also rose in April.

Industry sources estimated that about 500 billion yen ($4.00 billion) worth of foreign bonds of the types preferred by individual investors were issued in April, and they expected this pace to continue or even pick up speed in the months ahead.
"Unless the yen's weakeness is reversed and domestic short-term interest rates embark on a rising trend, such an increase is possible," said a brokerage source.
He said brokers have become increasingly dependent on revenues from underwriting foreign instruments to individuals amid sluggish demand for stocks.
The Yamaichi manager added that retail investors have become more eager to invest in foreign bonds in order to obtain higher yields at a time when Japanese interest rates are at record low levels.

"The strong interest in foreign bonds from retail investors is based on the wide gap in interest rates between Japan and foreign countries, so demand (for foreign bond issues) is likely to remain strong as long as Japan's ultra-low interest rates remain," he said.

A manager of the Treasury Department at a Japanese securities house said: "The bonus season is coming up and demand for dollar buying from Japanese investors (in connection with foreign bond issues) will continue to emerge."
Despite the dollar's retreat from a recent 56-month high of 127.47 yen and increases in Japanese bond yields, dealers do not think that demand for foreign bonds will wane anytime soon.
The dollar traded around 125.60/70 yen in afternoon Tokyo trade on Wednesday.

"We have seen steady dollar buying orders from securities houses regardless of the dollar's level," said Kouichi Murakami, senior manager of the financial engineering department at Sumitomo Trust & Banking Co Ltd.
He added that foreign bonds are likely to remain the investment product that Japanese securities houses market most aggressively to retail investors.
"In that sense, the dollar's downside remains solid," Murakami said.
